item.title: AI Literacy at Work: Implications for Human Resource Management
item.content:encoded:
Maarten Renkema, University of Twente

Laura Lamers, University of Twente

Christoph Lutz, BI Norwegian Business School

Anna B. Holm, Aarhus University

Artificial intelligence (AI) is being rapidly adopted across organisations, driven by promises of effectiveness and efficiency, yet accompanied by well-documented risks such as algorithmic bias and opacity. As competitive pressures compel AI adoption regardless, AI literacy—defined as the knowledge, skills, and attitudes that allow individuals (i.e., employees and HR-professionals) to engage effectively and critically with AI technologies—becomes crucial. This urgency is further underscored by the EU's AI Act, which includes the requirement for a sufficient level of AI literacy in organisations.

AI literacy research stands at a critical point. While widely acknowledged as necessary, it remains insufficiently understood in organisational and HRM contexts. Extant research on AI literacy has produced conceptual frameworks and measurement tools, but this work is predominantly embedded in educational research and is focused on individual learners, leaving the organisational perspective largely under-researched and under-theorised.

Appel publié par The International Journal of Human Resource Management. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Implications of AI literacy for core HRM functions, systems, policies and practices, including recruitment and selection, learning and development, performance management, and employee well-being
  • Organizational AI literacy: definition, design, implementation, and governance of HRM activities
  • Emergence mechanisms of individual AI literacy into collective organizational capability and HRM contributions
  • Relationship between organizational AI literacy and adjacent constructs such as organizational AI readiness, antecedents and outcomes
  • Competition for AI talent in the labour market and inequality implications inter- and intra-organizationally
  • Team reshaping and creation to enable, develop and foster AI literacy
  • HRM and HRD practices supporting development of AI-literate teams through workforce planning, staffing, job design, training and allocation of responsibilities
  • AI literacy levels and combinations needed across different teams and roles, and HRM practices supporting capability building
  • Manifestation of AI literacy in everyday work practices and its transformation of work
  • Technical, ethical and practical dimensions of AI literacy in AI-mediated recruitment, fairness perceptions, and AI overreliance
  • AI literacy of HR professionals and influence on adoption of AI tools

item.title: Addressing Ultra-Low Fertility and Workforce Shrinkage: A Human-Centered HRM Response to the Demographic Crisis
item.content:encoded:
Ingyu Oh, Kansai Gaidai University

Jie Wu, University of Aberdeen

Ho Kwong Kwan, China Europe International Business School

Hyun Jeong Kim, Inha University

Low fertility is emerging as a critical challenge in international human resource management (HRM). Ultra-low fertility—defined as a total fertility rate (TFR) of 1.3 or lower—is no longer confined to East Asia. It is now present across diverse regions, including parts of Southern and Eastern Europe (e.g., Italy, Spain, Poland), high-income Asian economies (e.g., South Korea, Japan, Singapore), and is increasingly affecting advanced economies in North America and Oceania. As of 2022, around 20 countries face ultra-low fertility, while 152 nations fall below the replacement level of 2.1.

This demographic crisis is transforming HRM from a support function into a strategic imperative. Policymakers around the world are sounding the alarm—South Korea warns of 'national extinction,' Japan calls it a 'quiet emergency,' and several European nations are grappling with labor market stagnation. The risks of shrinking workforces, declining productivity, and rising costs for talent acquisition and retention are now central economic concerns.

Appel publié par The International Journal of Human Resource Management. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Work-Life Balance Challenges: Family-friendly HRM policies and workplace cultures affecting fertility decisions
  • Work-Life Balance Challenges: Gender inequality, maternity/paternity leave, and childcare support impacts on career and family planning
  • Work-Life Balance Challenges: Cultural expectations and traditional gender roles influencing fertility rates
  • Work-Life Balance Challenges: Implementing on-site childcare, generous parental leave, and financial incentives for families
  • Work-Life Balance Challenges: Fostering inclusive environments prioritizing work-life balance and psychological safety
  • Adapting HR Practices: Flexible work policies including remote work, reduced hours, and enhanced parental leave
  • Adapting HR Practices: Upskilling and reskilling programs addressing workforce shrinkage
  • Adapting HR Practices: Inclusive benefits such as childcare support, eldercare programs, and fertility treatments
  • Adapting HR Practices: Diversity and inclusion strategies tapping underutilized labor pools (older workers, women, immigrants)
  • Adapting HR Practices: Innovative international recruitment strategies and talent pipeline development
  • Human-Centered AI Solutions: Deploying AI tools enhancing productivity without undermining employee wellbeing or autonomy
  • Human-Centered AI Solutions: AI-assisted work-life balance through predictive analytics and personalized leave planning
  • Human-Centered AI Solutions: AI-facilitated servant leadership and psychological safety reducing family planning fears
  • Human-Centered AI Solutions: AI-driven personalized work schedules for dual-earner couples
  • Human-Centered AI Solutions: Digital twin modeling simulating and optimizing career-family pathways
  • Human-Centered AI Solutions: AI and automation addressing labor shortages and optimizing workforce management
  • Rethinking Core HRM Theories: Developing scarcity-based view and demographic agility in HRM
  • Rethinking Core HRM Theories: Human capital preservation and the demographic premium concept
  • Institutional and Cultural Complexity: Reconciling global HR best practices with local fertility norms
  • Institutional and Cultural Complexity: Institutional fertility regimes and institutional entrepreneurship in gender-equity reforms
  • Institutional and Cultural Complexity: Cultural paradoxes and the influence of cultural tightness-looseness on policy uptake

item.title: Beyond AI: HRM and the Work of the Future
item.content:encoded:
Sandra Fisher, FH Münster

Janet Marler, University at Albany - SUNY

The 10th e-HRM Conference in Muenster, Germany (June 2026) provided a platform for scholars from around the world to share research and leading-edge insights into electronic/digital human resource management in the midst of another major technological revolution. This special issue highlights key research papers presented at the conference and also invites authors who were unable to attend the conference to submit their related research to this special issue.

item.title: Digital Nomadism and the Future of HRM: Rethinking Work, Workforce, and Workplace
item.content:encoded:
Matej Černe, University of Ljubljana

Marko Orel, Prague University of Economics and Business

Fabiola Mancinelli, University of Barcelona

Stefanie Reissner, Durham University

Brian Harney, Dublin City University

Digital nomadism combines location-independent, digitally mediated work with sustained or recurring geographic mobility. It has often been discussed as a lifestyle, tourism, migration, or mobility phenomenon, including in research on transformational travel, destination ecosystems, workation practices, and digital nomad visas. Yet, digital nomadism also raises central questions for human resource management: how organizations attract, organize, support, govern, develop, and retain workers whose employment relationships, work locations, and social embeddedness are increasingly fluid. This special issue invites HRM scholarship that treats digital nomadism as both a distinctive empirical setting and an analytically powerful context for rethinking work, workforce, and workplace in an international and digitally mediated economy.

Appel publié par The International Journal of Human Resource Management. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Work design, job demands and resources, autonomy, flexibility, isolation, insecurity, time-zone dispersion, infrastructure variability, and performance
  • Leadership, coordination, voice, psychological safety, performance management, and feedback in mobile and distributed work arrangements
  • The implications of digitalization, AI, algorithmic management, and digital platforms for where, how, and under what contractual conditions work is performed
  • Talent attraction, selection, retention, and employer branding for mobile and location-independent workers
  • Careers, employability, career self-management, protean careers, sustainable careers, and boundaryless or globally mobile talent pathways
  • Wellbeing, recovery, work-nonwork boundaries, social embeddedness, loneliness, identity, and community among digital nomads and other mobile workers
  • Onboarding, socialization, belonging, organizational identification, informal learning, and knowledge sharing when workers are geographically mobile
  • Destination ecosystems, coworking spaces, local communities, employers, governments, and intermediaries as actors shaping mobile digital work
  • Comparative research on digital nomadism across countries, regions, sectors, occupations, employment forms, and regulatory regimes
  • Employment relationships, psychological contracts, commitment, fairness, inclusion, and duty of care in remote, freelance, contractual, hybrid, or employee-based arrangements
  • International HRM, global mobility, digital nomad visas, taxation, labor law, social security, cross-border compliance, data protection, and institutional complexity
  • HR architecture and governance: balancing flexibility, autonomy, coordination, control, equity, risk management, and organizational support

item.title: Managing the digitally-savvy workforce: Human Resource Management in an evolving digital landscape
item.content:encoded:
Sanjay Singh, University of Dundee

Sateesh Shet, Northumbria University

Tanya Bondarouk, The University of Twente

Paresha Sinha, University of Waikato

James Duggan, Cork University Business School

The acceleration of digital transformation across industries has reshaped the nature of work and the workforce. In this evolving landscape, a new kind of employee has emerged, one that is digitally fluent, technology-enabled, and increasingly reliant on digital tools to perform, collaborate, and innovate. This digitally-savvy workforce brings with it a unique set of expectations, behaviors, and capabilities that are fundamentally altering traditional models of Human Resource Management.

As organizations navigate this shift, HRM must move beyond conventional practices to align with the realities of a workforce deeply embedded in digital ecosystems. The integration of emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence, machine learning, virtual collaboration platforms, and HR analytics is not only transforming operational HR functions but also reshaping strategic priorities around talent acquisition, workforce planning, performance management, employee engagement, and learning and development.

Appel publié par The International Journal of Human Resource Management. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Strategic workforce planning for the digital era, including forecasting digital talent needs, digital upskilling frameworks, and bridging digital skills gaps
  • Work design for digitally enabled workforce, encompassing job roles in technology-mediated environments, digital flexibility, autonomy, work-life integration, and remote work impacts
  • Emerging digital technologies and HRM transformation, including AI, blockchain, virtual reality, chatbots, intelligent automation, and HR digital twins
  • Redefining talent acquisition for digitally-savvy workforce through social media recruitment, gamified assessments, AI in recruitment, and employer branding
  • Performance management in tech-driven organizations, covering digital dashboards, algorithmic evaluation, surveillance, real-time feedback, and fairness implications
  • Employee engagement and experience in digital workspaces, including digital platforms, AI-driven personalization, digital fatigue, and tech-enabled burnout
  • Ethics, privacy, and surveillance in digital workplace, addressing algorithmic monitoring, employee autonomy, and ethical HR technology adoption
  • Inclusion, equity, and accessibility in digital HR practices, focusing on digital exclusion reduction, neurodiverse talent support, and fair AI-driven decision-making

item.title: The Institutional Fragility of Inclusion in Contemporary HRM Systems
item.content:encoded:
Benjamin Laker, Henley Business School, University of Reading

Sven Horak, St. John's University

Toyin Ajibade Adisa, Royal Docks School of Business and Law, University of East London

Fulya Acikgoz, University of Sussex Business School

Inclusion has become a defining aspiration in modern human resource management. It is embedded in recruitment policies, leadership development strategies, employee engagement programmes, and organisational values. Yet, the institutional standing of inclusion is increasingly precarious. Across sectors and geographies, political retrenchment, economic turbulence, organisational ambivalence, and cultural contestation have converged to destabilise the norms and mechanisms that once sustained inclusive HRM.

This special issue examines the institutional fragility of inclusion—a condition in which inclusion is publicly endorsed but inconsistently enacted, weakly governed, or symbolically maintained in the absence of substantive commitment. In this context, we ask: What becomes of workplace inclusion when its institutional scaffolding weakens, but identity difference endures—embodied, politicised, and inescapable?

Appel publié par The International Journal of Human Resource Management. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Organisational responses to the erosion or contestation of inclusion mandates
  • Identity construction, negotiation, and resistance within HRM systems
  • Symbolic inclusion vs substantive change in HRM practice and policy
  • How performance systems, leadership pipelines, or 'culture fit' criteria embed normative assumptions about who belongs
  • Comparative and global analyses of inclusion across varied institutional, legal, and cultural settings
  • HRM as a mechanism of voice suppression, identity masking, or strategic silence
  • The effects of intersectional identity configurations (e.g. gender × race × class) on access to opportunity, recognition, and legitimacy in HRM
  • How informal networks and shadow structures sustain or subvert inclusion efforts
  • Experiences of inclusion and exclusion when organisations retreat from formal DEI commitments
  • Institutional logics, power asymmetries, and the politics of belonging in HRM systems
  • Decolonial or Indigenous critiques of Western-centric inclusion frameworks in global HRM

Timeline

  • November 30, 2026: Manuscript deadline

item.title: The Interplay of Human Resource Management and Leadership: Alignment, Tensions, and Consequences
item.content:encoded:
Aneeqa Suhail, Tilburg University

Steven Kilroy, Trinity College Dublin

Robin Bauwens, Tilburg University

Sut I Wong, BI Norwegian Business School

Sasa Batistič, Tilburg University

Managing people in organizations requires a combination of Human Resource Management (HRM) and leadership, often referred to as 'people management'. While HRM provides formalized systems, practices, and architectures that structure employment relationships, leadership shapes how these systems are enacted, interpreted, and given meaning in everyday work. Therefore, the outcomes traditionally associated with people management do not emerge from HRM or leadership in isolation, but from their ongoing interrelationship across organizational levels.

Appel publié par The International Journal of Human Resource Management. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • How HRM systems and leadership behaviors interact in shaping employee and organizational outcomes across organizational levels
  • How different forms of alignment between HRM and leadership (e.g., supplementary fit, complementary fit, perceptual filtering) produce distinct employee and organizational outcomes
  • When and how HRM systems function as substitutes for leadership, and what are the resulting consequences for employee and organizational outcomes
  • How misalignment between HRM systems and leadership behaviors emerge, persist, or become institutionalized within organizations
  • When alignment between HRM systems and leadership amplifies negative outcomes such as work intensification, role overload, or employee strain
  • How employees interpret and respond to situations in which HRM systems substitute for, constrain, or contradict leadership behaviors
  • Which configurations of HRM systems and leadership forms strengthen the effectiveness and sustainability of remote and hybrid work arrangements
  • How leaders enact, adapt, or resist HRM systems when leading employees at a distance, and how does this shape employees' sensemaking and experiences of people management
  • How employees experience alignment, misalignment, or substitution between HRM systems and leadership in remote and hybrid work settings, and how do these experiences affect employee and organizational outcomes
  • How HRM–leadership configurations evolve over time and how do these experiences affect pertinent employee and organizational outcomes
  • How alignment, misalignment, and substitution between HRM and leadership shape employee well-being and performance over time
  • How temporal shifts in leadership behaviors or HRM systems alter the balance between substitution and complementarity
